name: Pawpaw
habitat: Clonal understory patches in rich, moist bottomland forest and shady river and creek terraces; native to 26 states from northern Florida to southern Ontario and west to eastern Nebraska. Large drooping leaves and a tropical look give the patch away long before the fruit does.
parts: Ripe pulp only, raw or in custards and ice cream — banana-mango-custard flavour. Ripe fruit yields to a gentle tug and gives softly under the thumb. Do NOT eat the skin or the big brown seeds: NC State attributes stomach and intestinal pain to eating skin or seeds, notes the acetogenins in the plant, and lists contact dermatitis from handling fruit. A minority of people get a GI or allergic reaction to the pulp itself, so try a small amount the first time.
harvest: Never pull unripe fruit — it will not ripen properly and you have wasted it. Pick only fruit that releases with a light tug, or shake the small tree and take what drops. Patches are clonal and self-incompatible, so fruit set is often poor; take a share and leave the rest, and don't cut or break branches to reach clusters.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program (harvest late August to mid-October; ripe fruit yields to a gentle tug): https://www.kysu.edu/academics/college-ahnr/school-of-anr/pawpaw/
NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Asimina triloba (skin/seed toxicity, acetogenins, contact dermatitis): https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/asimina-triloba/
